analysis:
Supplied units are BASE-side text only (lines 1726-2600) of ClusterOnboardingLive.swift. The changed ranges, from file_changes, touch pairServing's loop (base 2217/2223-2224), pairStopped (2286-2289), the leaderStatus routed call (2360-2361), stop (2519), and localStop (2546-2563). The head-side text was not supplied, and the patch excerpt is truncated. The visible patch hunks add stopsAsked and serve(unlessStoppedSince:) closures, followerStatus (which adds stopsAsked to the status reply), and ClusterControlRequest.stopsBefore. Together these appear to be a stop-versus-serve race guard on the intra-cluster control link. I could not verify that the head code is safe.

What the base text shows: the cluster onboarding and control path is a local, owner-run CLI/UX flow between two paired Macs. It makes no changes to the coordinator-to-provider WebSocket, the E2E encryption of A-001, the attestation chain (TB-009), or the prefix cache (T-041). The retrieved T-041 relates only to the KV cache, which this file does not touch. Base localStop (2552-2591) records stopDrain, drains the local part, then asks the peer to stop. A stopsBefore counter received over the link and used to decide whether to serve is a new field in the peer-control message. The authentication of that link (control channel, leaderID) is outside this unit.

No concrete security regression is supported by the supplied evidence. Open questions for integration: (1) Is the new stopsBefore/stopsAsked value, which a follower sends to the leader, authenticated and bounded, so that a peer cannot suppress or force a serve? (2) Does serve(unlessStoppedSince:) fail closed, i.e. never serve after a user stop? (3) Is the persisted counter in the store record tamper-resistant under the TB-003 same-user assumptions? Because head text and the full patch were not supplied, I am requesting deeper review of the head side.
